layer1_philosophy.methodology: A gentle, Christian, literature-rich preschool rhythm for ages 3 to 5. Each alphabet letter anchors one week of read-alouds, multisensory phonics, real-object counting, fine and large motor work, practical life, process art, and a Friday field trip. Montessori-influenced elements include a prepared environment, tactile letters, practical life, and the Three Period Lesson. Living books, narration, short lessons, nature, and beauty overlap with Charlotte Mason practice, but the source does not present itself as a complete Montessori or Charlotte Mason program.
principles: Use hands-on experiences before expecting later abstract skills.
Let the child's comfort and developmental pace govern repetition, skipping, and session length.
Prepare an orderly, beautiful, natural home environment that makes independent activity accessible.
Teach letter sounds before emphasizing letter names, using tactile tracing, clay, salt, and real objects.
Teach early mathematics with manipulatives and real household quantities.
Place movement between quieter tasks because large motor work supports attention and learning.
Build self-respect and independence through real work in the home.
Use picture books, poems, Bible stories and verses, narration, nature, art, music, cooking, and field trips as one connected week.
Model first, invite recognition second, and ask for recall only when the child is ready.
Keep devices off during ordinary preschool life and preserve free exploration, responsive care, and healthy rhythms.

layer1_philosophy.learningTheory: Developmentally paced, multisensory, experiential, relationship-centered learning with modeling, repetition, free exploration, prepared-environment independence, and cumulative alphabet review.
layer1_philosophy.assessmentApproach: Observation only. Use the kindergarten readiness checklist periodically, notice what the child can do comfortably, repeat or skip activities, and never convert the checklist into a verdict or pressure to keep pace.
layer1_philosophy.parentRole: Act as a responsive model, environment-setter, read-aloud partner, narrator-listener, practical-life guide, and field-trip companion. Demonstrate an activity, invite the child to try, help only as needed, and stop or switch when attention and comfort say the session is done.

knowledgeBankGaps.title: Peaceful Preschool alphabet rhythm format
knowledgeBankGaps.summary: A 26-week, ages 3 to 5 home-preschool rhythm in which one alphabet letter anchors four short activity days and a Friday field trip. Every week joins living read-alouds, tactile letter-sound work, real-object counting, fine motor practice, movement, practical life, process art, optional cooking, and a theme.
knowledgeBankGaps.content: Prepare accessible trays, real tools, picture books, tactile letters, counting objects, art materials, and a calm daily rhythm. On Monday through Thursday, read one book, poem, Bible story, or verse; model the week's sound with glitter-glue, clay, salt, and object matching; count and classify real things; alternate fine and large motor work; complete one useful home task; and make art connected to the literature or theme. Invite narration without forcing it. Friday becomes a local field trip or simple shared celebration. Keep each activity brief, repeat what engages the child, skip what does not fit, and stretch the 26 weeks across 52 weeks when two activity days per week better fit the family.

layer2_scope.taxonomyRuling: All 27 curriculum concepts now map to concrete taxonomy topics. Fine and gross motor work route into Homa's existing motor subjects through separate content domains, so they do not collide with scored assessment domains. Biblical story and verse familiarity remains a parked, content-only Religious Education subject, and a child's beliefs are never scored. No prerequisite edge was justified.

layer3_structure.cadence: Twenty-six alphabet weeks. Monday through Thursday each include a read-aloud, phonics, counting, fine motor, large motor, practical life, and art. Friday is a field trip or shared celebration. Families may instead complete two activity days per week and spread the sequence across 52 weeks.
layer3_structure.cadenceEvidence: with Fridays set aside for field trips.

sessionLengthMinutes.note: The source recommends stopping after about five minutes when that better fits the child and does not prescribe a fixed daily total.
sessionLengthMinutes.evidence: It is better to spend 5 minutes doing an activity

layer3_structure.weeklyTemplate: Read one picture book, poem, Bible story or verse; model and review the letter sound with glitter glue, salt, clay, tracing, and real-object matching; count, sort, compare, or measure real things; complete fine motor and large motor work; practice one useful home skill; make art or cook around the theme; then use Friday for a related local outing or gathering.
layer3_structure.progressionModel: Linear A-to-Z letter sequence with cumulative review. Previously introduced letters, quantities, movement patterns, self-care tasks, and chores recur, while the parent adjusts difficulty to readiness.
layer3_structure.reviewRhythm: Daily tactile letter review and real-object practice, weekly cumulative alphabet flash or clay review, recurring narration and practical-life rehearsal, periodic observation through the kindergarten skills checklist, and no formal tests.

Form and trace letters in salt, sand, clay, chalk, and other sensory media.
Count, compare, group, add, subtract, and match numerals with real household, food, toy, and nature objects.
Sort objects by one observable attribute such as size, color, type, or family.
Teach a real home-care or self-care sequence and let the child repeat it with accessible tools.
Turn family essentials, morning routines, books, physical activity, and rest into a simple visible rhythm.
Use transferring, lacing, tonging, pinning, cutting, sewing, modeling, and hand-strengthening invitations.
Use crawling, rolling, balancing, hopping, skipping, throwing, catching, climbing, and dramatic movement between quieter tasks.
Make child-led watercolor, collage, clay, print, nature, and book-inspired art with a short materials and process guide.
Create masks, puppets, kites, books, models, and themed props from simple household craft materials.
Take a short outdoor walk, observe seasonal plants or animals, gather nature items, and draw or sort what was found.
Prepare a simple related local outing, observation focus, and short follow-up conversation or art response.
